title: the summit sit
hook: a bronze dancer in a glass case, one foot planted, one foot lifted, and everything in between meaning something

segments.voice: Yesterday, the summit sit looked back at Shakti, and a snake that is one snake whether it's coiled or moving. Did you catch something still moving in you at a still moment? Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.
screen: `THE SUMMIT SIT.` · `ONE SNAKE, STILL OR MOVING.`

segments.voice: A glass case in a quiet gallery. Inside, a bronze figure stands in a ring of flames. One foot is planted. The other is lifted and swung across. Hair flies out to the sides as if the figure just spun. People walk past it with their phones out and walk on. But on this path, a whole week went into standing in front of that figure and reading it, one hand at a time. Today the summit sit goes back to Shiva as Nataraja, the lord of the dance, and reads him all at once.
screen: `A BRONZE IN A RING OF FIRE.` → `ONE FOOT DOWN, ONE FOOT LIFTED.` → `READ IT ALL AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Back in the Nataraja week, each day took one piece. Now put the pieces back together. In one hand, a small drum, and in the tradition, its beat is the sound of things beginning. In the hand across from it, a flame: the ending, held level with the beginning, neither one higher. Another hand is raised, palm out, in the gesture that says do not fear. Another arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk, and the hand at its end doesn't grab. It points down, toward the lifted foot. Under the planted foot lies a small figure on his belly, and the dancer keeps him there without ever finishing him off. Caught in the streaming hair, there's a tiny figure with folded hands: the river Ganga, slowed and held. Tamil Shaiva teaching reads the whole figure as the god's work in the world: making, keeping, ending, concealing, and grace. And here's what's easy to miss while you're studying one hand at a time. None of these happen one after another. The drum doesn't wait for the flame. The ending is already in the room while the beginning is sounding. The fear-not hand is raised in the middle of the fire. The figure is one moment, and everything is in it. That's worth carrying down from the summit. A week, a year, a life doesn't arrive in neat chapters. Beginnings and endings share the same body. And this week, the week now closing, did that too: the last of the regions, Punjab's shared ground, ended just as the summit sits began.
screen: `THE DRUM AND THE FLAME, LEVEL.` · `FEAR NOT, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FIRE.` · `THE HAND THAT POINTS TO THE FOOT.` · `EVERYTHING IN ONE MOMENT.` · then, large: `BEGINNINGS AND ENDINGS SHARE A BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one moment with everything in it. Sit, and let the breath come. Notice that each breath is already ending as it begins: the in-breath turning, the out-breath turning. Then let the week come to mind, all of it at once, not in order. Something that began this week. Something that ended. Something you were afraid of. Let them stand together, the way the drum and the flame are held level. If you pray, you can rest before Shiva, the dancer, with all of it. The bell holds the time.
The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Nataraja, read all at once, with the drum and the flame held level. Today's word.

Your line: the summit sit. Today, when something ends, a meeting, a meal, the week, notice what is beginning in the same moment. This week closes as the summit sits begin. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Nataraja is worshiped in temples and homes, notably at Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, and the figure is honored in classical dance, where dancers often begin by saluting him.

fork.setup: you're reading the bronze. one arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk. where does its hand point?
fork.reveal: it points to the lifted foot. the hand doesn't grab anything; it shows the way.

notes: Summit sit, day 3: revisits 'Nataraja explained' (1125–1131). Week end (1414 = week of 1408–1414), so the teach and carry look back at the week: the end of Punjab's shared devotional ground and the start of the summit sits.

Iconography summarized: damaru (drum) as the sound of creation; fire in the opposite hand; abhaya hand; gaja-hasta arm pointing to the raised foot; the figure under the planted foot (Apasmara/Muyalakan) held, not killed; Ganga in the hair. The 'making, keeping, ending, concealing, grace' reading is the five acts (pancakritya) of Shaiva Siddhanta; the source is given generally. Confirm the attribution to Unmai Vilakkam or replace with a better reference.
